summary:
Suriname has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct since 1869, and that position applies to men and women nationwide. Following the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the Penal Code was revised so that the age of consent is the same for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

In March 2015 Articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were revised to reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation. Whether those provisions extend to gender identity is not stated in the sources available here.

Protection otherwise rests on an implied reading rather than an express statute. Article 8.2 of the Constitution of Suriname lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds.

Legal gender recognition is not available. A trans visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with their presentation should expect document checks to be difficult rather than routine, and the sources available here do not describe how Surinamese border authorities handle such documents.

Formal protection has not produced safe conditions. A July 2024 civil-society report filed with the UN Human Rights Committee records that LGBTI people face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation despite constitutional protection, and the US State Department's 2015 human rights report documented discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities in Suriname.

Registration of LGBTI organisations is permitted. The Surinamese state told the Human Rights Committee in July 2024 that its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, with monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission in place; committee experts pressed the delegation on implementation of a regional court's judgment concerning transgender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Police conduct forms part of the risk picture: the US State Department's 2015 report documented police brutality and corruption alongside its findings on minority discrimination. The same report recorded the trial of President Bouterse, evidence of a wider climate of institutional strain rather than a trans-specific measure.

Suriname abolished the death penalty in the Penal Code in 2015 and in the Military Code in 2021, a point the Human Rights Committee welcomed at its July 2024 review. This bears on the severity of the criminal system a visitor enters, not on trans status specifically.

Civil-society access to decision-making is contested. The Suriname LGBT Platform reported to the UN in March 2016 that it had been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests, which limits how much weight official statements of protection carry in practice.
localsOnly:
LGBT Platform Suriname was founded on 29 August 2011 and unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action. The platform, together with the Projekta Foundation and VIDS, published a civil-society report in July 2024; submissions to the UN Human Rights Committee have also been made jointly with Heartland Alliance and Akahata.

Residents can register LGBTI organisations, and the platform and its allies have repeatedly called for a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability. No such statute is in force; the constitutional 'any other status' clause remains the operative hook, supplemented by the March 2015 Penal Code amendments on sexual-orientation discrimination and hate speech.

Discrimination complaints are handled through monitoring machinery including the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, which the state cited during the July 2024 Human Rights Committee review as evidence of enforcement capacity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans visitors are not covered by the source inventory and remain unresolved here, including any requirement to disclose gender identity or prior name on arrival documentation.

Whether the March 2015 Penal Code provisions on discrimination and hate speech have ever been applied in a prosecution, and with what outcome, is not sourced. Enforcement of the constitutional 'any other status' reading through the courts is likewise unresolved.

The precise content of the regional court judgment on transgender identity that experts pressed Suriname to implement in July 2024 is not described in the inventory; the deadline or status of implementation is not sourced.

Facilities access, healthcare restrictions and partner recognition for trans visitors are absent from the available sources. The inventory confirms only that legal gender recognition is not possible.
